context: tank erection & hydrotest-led · fire/foam protection is safety-critical

brief.intro: New to this project type? A tank farm (bulk liquid storage terminal) is a cluster of large field-erected storage tanks joined by transfer piping to a jetty, pipeline or truck-loading rack, all wrapped in fire protection. The building work is minimal — the real scope is welding steel tank shells plate by plate on a ring-beam foundation, then proving every weld holds before a drop of product goes in. Your schedule is driven by tank plate and roof-structure fabrication and delivery, the erect-then-test sequence for each tank (bottom → shell → roof → NDE → hydrotest → settlement survey), and the foam/deluge fire-protection system that must be proven before any tank is put into service.

scope.name: Site & civil works
scope.desc: Earthworks, tank ring-beam foundations, bund/secondary-containment walls and access/haul roads.

scope.name: Tank fabrication & erection
scope.desc: Bottom plate, shell courses and roof structure built up per API 650, tank by tank.

scope.name: Welding, NDE & hydrotest
scope.desc: Weld inspection, radiography and a water-fill hydrotest with settlement survey before any tank enters service.

scope.name: Transfer piping & pipe racks
scope.desc: Interconnecting process piping, manifolds and tie-ins to jetty, pipeline or truck-loading systems.

scope.name: Rotating equipment
scope.desc: Transfer and product pumps — set, aligned and run-in.

scope.name: Fire protection
scope.desc: Fixed foam and deluge systems, hydrants and monitors protecting each tank and the bund.

scope.name: Electrical & cathodic protection
scope.desc: Power distribution, earthing/bonding and cathodic protection against tank-shell corrosion.

scope.name: Instrumentation & tank gauging
scope.desc: Automatic tank gauging (ATG), independent overfill protection and temperature/pressure instruments.

scope.name: Insulation & coating
scope.desc: External corrosion coating and, on heated or refrigerated product tanks, insulation.

scope.name: Testing, commissioning & handover
scope.desc: Functional test of fire systems, first product-in and handover to operations.

glossary.plain: the design-and-construction (and later in-service inspection) code that governs how atmospheric storage tank shells are built.
the reinforced-concrete ring the tank bottom sits on and is anchored to.
one ring of vertical steel plates welded together to make up the tank wall — tanks are built course by course, bottom to top.
filling the empty tank with water to prove the shell and every weld is leak-free before real product goes in.
a level survey that checks how much, and how evenly, a filled tank has sunk into its foundation.
the walled, impervious area around a tank (or group of tanks) sized to hold a spill.
the fixed fire-fighting system that blankets a tank fire in foam or floods it with water.
automatic level instruments, backed by an independent high-level trip, that stop a tank being overfilled.
a low-voltage electrical system that stops the tank's buried or wetted steel corroding.

must_get_right: Sequence each tank bottom → shell → roof with weld NDE gates between courses — rework after roof closure is slow and expensive.
Hydrotest and settlement-survey every tank before its piping tie-in — a failed test after tie-in means cutting pipework back out.
Prove the foam/deluge fire system functional before any tank is commissioned into service — it is the safety gate, not an afterthought.
Keep the bund/secondary containment complete and tested ahead of first product-in — it is usually a regulatory precondition, not just good practice.

basis_of_planning.standard: AACE Recommended Practice 38R-06 — Documenting the Schedule Basis

sections.heading: Scheduling method & tools
sections.body: A Critical Path Method (CPM) network built in Primavera P6, developed to a Level 3 control schedule with retained-logic progress. Each tank is broken out as its own activity string (foundation → erection → NDE → hydrotest) so tank-by-tank progress and float are visible separately.

sections.heading: Calendars & working time
sections.body: Civil and tank-erection work a 6-day week; hydrotest and settlement-survey activities carry fixed non-workable durations (water hold, settlement monitoring period) that cannot be compressed by adding resources. Fire-system testing and commissioning run a standard calendar.

sections.heading: Sequencing logic & critical path
sections.body: The driving path runs ring-beam foundation → tank bottom/shell/roof erection → weld NDE → hydrotest & settlement survey → piping tie-in → fire-system proving → product-in. The largest-diameter or last-delivered tank in the farm typically governs, since the transfer piping and the fire ring main cannot be proven complete until every tank in the group is tied in.

sections.heading: Key assumptions
sections.body: Design is frozen and the tank layout/spacing approved per the applicable fire code; tank plate and roof-structure fabrication drawings are released for shop fabrication ahead of foundation completion; a single mobilisation; ring-beam foundations are load-tested/cured before tank erection starts. Any change to these invalidates the baseline dates.

sections.heading: Access, resource & site constraints
sections.body: Heavy-lift cranes for roof structures and skilled, code-qualified tank welders are shared across tanks and are a resource constraint when several tanks erect in parallel; hot-work permits inside the bund are tightly controlled once adjacent tanks hold product.

sections.heading: Risks, float & contingency
sections.body: Principal risks: hydrotest/settlement-survey failure forcing repair and re-test, weld-repair rework discovered at NDE, and foam-system supply lead time. Schedule contingency is held immediately after each tank's hydrotest and again before the fire-system functional test, rather than spread thinly across erection activities.

sections.heading: Schedule levels of detail
sections.body: Reported at Level 1 (milestones) and Level 2 (summary) to the client, by tank; controlled at Level 3; expanded to Level 4–5 lookahead for the field — consistent with AACE 37R-06.
